terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with the accusative of the place
evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.87: Pȳthagorās et Aegyptum lustrāvit et Persārum magōs adiit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Morgan–Owens’s word for exploring lands. Its first sense is “purify” (by a sacrifice carried round), whence “go round”; it also means “survey, look over” (oculīs lustrāre) (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: go all through; look all over
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with the accusative
terms.comment: Go through every part of a place, or look it all over; Livy’s word, and Cicero’s for surveying a subject (Part. 38).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with the accusative
evidence: Verg. G. 4.53, of bees: saltūs silvāsque (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From per and ager: roam the length and breadth of a country.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with an accusative or an indirect question
evidence: Cic. Att. 6.8.5: explōrā rem tōtam (Lewis & Short)
Mor. 6: sollicitāque manū tenebrās explōrat inertēs
terms.comment: Not the English “explore” for travelling: it is to search out or try what is unknown, as a scout does, or a hand feeling its way in the dark, and so to look into a matter. Cicero uses it most in explōrātum, “certain, known for sure” (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Pȳthagorās et Aegyptum lustrāvit et Persārum magōs adiit
phrases.english: Pythagoras travelled all over Egypt and went to the Persian magi

phrases.latin: sollicitāque manū tenebrās explōrat inertēs vestīgatque focum
phrases.english: with an anxious hand he feels his way through the dark and searches for the hearth
